summary.text: Malleability is a material's ability to be formed cold by stamping or pressing instead of cracking.
In metals, valence electrons are shared between many atoms, so the atoms can slide past one another without strong repulsion.
Gold is the most malleable metal, while materials that crack or shatter under stress cannot be worked by hammering.

facts.label: Brittle materials instead
facts.value: They may be cast or thermoformed

facts.label: Beyond metals
facts.value: Many plastics and Play-Doh are malleable too

facts.label: Why metals give
facts.value: Shared electrons let atoms slide past each other

items.prompt: A workshop wants to shape pieces by squeezing them cold in a stamping press without any cracking. What property of the material makes that possible?

options.label: It can be formed cold by pressing without breaking
It is brittle, so it keeps a rigid shape under force
It melts easily, so it flows into the die
It is hard enough to resist any change of shape

items.explain: Malleable materials can be formed cold by stamping or pressing, while materials that crack under stress cannot be shaped this way.

items.prompt: A material cracks and shatters under stress. Which way of shaping it fits best?

options.label: Rolling it into thin sheets
Casting it or thermoforming it
Hammering it flat while cold
Pressing it in a stamp at room temperature

items.explain: Materials that crack or shatter cannot be hammered or rolled, so brittle materials are cast or thermoformed instead.

items.prompt: Why can the atoms in a piece of metal slide past each other without the metal shattering?

options.label: Each atom grips its electrons tightly, locking neighbours in place
Metal atoms are much lighter than the atoms of other materials
Outer electrons are shared among many atoms, so little repulsion builds up
Metal atoms sit in a rigid lattice that never lets them move

items.explain: In metallic bonds the valence electrons are delocalized and shared between many atoms, so atoms slide without the strong repulsion that would shatter other materials.

items.prompt: A jeweller wants the metal that can be pressed into shape most easily of all. Which fits?

options.label: Platinum
Copper
Cast iron
Gold

items.explain: Gold is the most malleable metal. Platinum is the most ductile of the pure metals, which is a different claim, and cast iron fails in a brittle way.

items.prompt: A child flattens a lump of Play-Doh into a pancake and it does not break. What does this show about malleability?

options.label: Only metals can change shape this way
Some plastics and other non-metals can be malleable too
That dough must contain metallic bonds
Malleable and brittle mean the same thing

items.explain: Many plastics and amorphous solids, such as Play-Doh, are also malleable, so malleability is not limited to metals.

items.prompt: A ceramic plate cracks into pieces when it is dropped. What best explains this?

options.label: Strong bonds hold its atoms in a rigid, packed lattice
Its atoms share electrons freely and slide past each other
Its atoms are held too loosely to keep any shape
Its bonds are weak, so any knock breaks them apart

items.explain: Ceramics are generally brittle because strong ionic or covalent bonds keep atoms in a rigid, densely packed lattice, which restricts the movement needed for plastic deformation.

paragraphs.heading: Why metals bend
paragraphs.text: High ductility comes from metallic bonds, which are found mostly in metals. In such a bond the outer, or valence, electrons are not tied to one atom; they are spread out and shared among many atoms. These shared electrons let metal atoms slide past each other without meeting the strong repulsion that would make other materials shatter. This is behind the common view that metals are ductile in general.

paragraphs.heading: Why ceramics break
paragraphs.text: Many inorganic materials, including a wide range of ceramics and semiconductors, are brittle instead. Their strong ionic or covalent bonds hold the atoms in a stiff, tightly packed arrangement. That rigid lattice restricts the movement of atoms and of dislocations, a kind of defect, which plastic deformation depends on. As a result, these materials usually stretch much less at room temperature than ductile metals do.

paragraphs.heading: Gold, platinum and steel
paragraphs.text: Among metals, gold is the most malleable, while among the pure metals platinum is the most ductile. Gold and copper are both commonly described as ductile. Not every metal behaves this way, though: cast iron, for example, tends to fail in a brittle way. Steel's ductility varies with its alloying ingredients, and raising the carbon content lowers it.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond metals
paragraphs.text: Many plastics and amorphous solids, Play-Doh among them, are malleable as well. Polymers are generally treated as ductile, since they usually allow plastic deformation. In engineering, ductility decides whether a material suits processes such as cold working. It also governs how well a part can absorb a mechanical overload, as in an engine.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it is tricky
paragraphs.text: One measure of ductility compares a sample's length after it fractures with its length before the test. The result commonly depends on the size and shape of the sample. Tests on the same material can give values that differ by a factor of two or three. For many purposes it is better to run a different test that measures toughness, the energy absorbed during fracture.
